chapter_theme: Neelakesi debates the Buddha himself: she charges that his store of consciousness is the soul under another name, argues that hearing is by contact and that a momentary mind could not understand a word or know anything, presses the difference between perception and consciousness, and then takes the Buddhist ten bad deeds in order, showing that the rules on coveting, anger, view, lying, slander and harsh or gentle speech do not hold as stated.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha, whom Neelakesi debates in person in this sarukkam

513.reading: Neelakesi says that when she argued the consciousnesses other than the one now manifest are gone, since nothing can be grasped of them, the Buddha answered that they rest in a store (ஆலயம்); by that name he has quietly taken back the soul.
513.nuance: The word ஆலயம் (line 3, doubled) answers to the Buddhist store-consciousness: Neelakesi's point is that a lasting receptacle of past knowings is the soul in all but name, the same move she made against Kundalakesi's carried-over power (203). Whether the Buddhists would accept the store as a soul is exactly what the Jain account denies them.

claims.claim: the consciousnesses not now manifest are kept in a store-consciousness
a lasting store of consciousness is the soul under another name

514.reading: Neelakesi likens the Buddha to a burglar who, saying he cannot be seen in the dark evening, digs into a rich man's house at broad noon: he keeps as his 'store' the precious soul the compassionate teach, and has lost his dignity in confusion.
514.nuance: The simile turns doctrine into theft: the soul belongs to அருளுடையார் (the compassionate, line 3, the Jains as Neelakesi presents them), and taking it in daylight under a new name is a theft everyone can see.

claims.claim: the store the Buddhist posits is the soul the Jain teachers teach

515.reading: Neelakesi takes up the Buddhist rule that nose, tongue and body know their three objects only when they strike against them, and asks how, if the knowing in these three is formless, it can take touches at all.
515.nuance: The Buddhist position reported is that smell, taste and touch are known by contact; the objection is that a formless knower cannot be struck. Line 3 (யாலாக்கிய, ஒருவாப் பாக்கியம்) is hard to construe, so the shape of the objection is read from lines 1-2 and 4.

claims.claim: nose, tongue and body know their objects only on contact with them
a formless knowing cannot receive contact

516.reading: Neelakesi says the Buddha teaches that the ear takes sound without its reaching it, but he has not learned the truth: we do not hear a thing at the moment we see it but afterwards, because sound must travel until it reaches its organ.
516.nuance: The argument is from experience: sight and sound of one event come apart in time, so the ear must wait for sound to arrive. பெருந்தவத்தாய் (line 3), 'man of great penance', is said in mockery.

claims.claim: the ear grasps sound without contact
sound is heard after the thing is seen because it must travel to the ear, so hearing is by contact

517.reading: The Buddha replies that if sound came and touched the ear it could not be heard as far off; Neelakesi answers that sound in the ear may still be known as from afar, and bids him understand.
517.nuance: Lines 3-4 are obscure: the comparison with the 'fire' of all-knowing knowledge (முற்றறிவின் தீத்தனை) cannot be fixed, so the shape of her answer is uncertain. The verse closes in the narrator's voice (தெருட்டினளே).
517.event: The Buddha objects that a sound heard as distant cannot touch the ear, and Neelakesi answers him.

claims.claim: if sound touched the ear it could not be heard as far away

518.reading: Neelakesi asks how, if the mind that grasped the first letter of a word perishes, anyone can understand a word whole and speak it, or learn and put together any reckoning at all.
518.nuance: The objection to momentariness is tested on the smallest case, a single word heard letter by letter. Line 1 (பிரிவின்கணாறாம் பெயர் நுனது, perhaps 'your name, its letters parted') is obscure.

claims.claim: the mind that grasps each letter perishes at once
understanding a word or a reckoning needs a knower that lasts across its parts

519.reading: Neelakesi argues that if the aggregates are called a soul only by their union, then to call him 'Buddha' for his awakening is a lie too, since the awakening belonged only to its first moment; he does not even know what he has attained.
519.nuance: She turns the Buddhist account of the self as a conventional name against the Buddha's own title: on that account no one persists to be the awakened one.

claims.claim: the soul is only a name for the union of the aggregates
if the self is only a name, the title Buddha names no one who awoke

520.reading: Neelakesi of the spreading hair, who speaks nothing but winning words, concludes that since the Buddha's words have no real things for their objects, she is now clear that he who spoke them has no knowledge at all.

claims.claim: words have no real objects
one whose words refer to nothing real has no knowledge

521.reading: Neelakesi announces that she will now explain the six perceptions (குறி), their objects and how they take them, and how perception differs from consciousness, without confusing the terms.
521.nuance: குறி here is the perception aggregate, not a sign: the next three verses press whether it can be told apart from knowing (உணர்வு), the point she made against Kundalakesi in 194.

522.reading: The woman whose speech outdoes a tune names the six perceptions: of eye, nose, body, ear, tongue and, with the mind, the perception that thinks.
522.nuance: காடின் (line 2) gives no sense and is probably corrupt; the sixth perception is read as the mind's.

claims.claim: perception is of six kinds, one for each of the five senses and the mind

523.reading: Neelakesi argues that if consciousness and perception have one and the same object they are one thing, and if each takes another object the difference can be shown; so she says.
523.nuance: The opening horn of a dilemma: two aggregates with a single object collapse into one, as she argued in 194 that feeling, perception and volition are not other than knowing.

claims.claim: two faculties that take the same object are not two

524.reading: Neelakesi presses the dilemma: if perception reaches its real object while consciousness does not, then either their object is one and they are one, or, if consciousness never meets it, consciousness has no object at all.
524.nuance: Lines 1-2 are compressed and the sense of உண்மைகுறி is not secure; the conclusion in line 4 is clear.

claims.claim: if consciousness does not reach the object perception takes, consciousness has no object

525.reading: Neelakesi argues that if perception and consciousness arise with their object at one instant and perish together, nothing is known, and if they do not arise together, then since the object arises at once there is still no knowing.
525.nuance: This is the momentariness objection in its sharpest form: a knowing that lasts no longer than its object has no time in which to know it.

claims.claim: object, perception and consciousness arise together and perish together
on that account nothing is ever known

526.reading: Neelakesi turns to the Buddhists' wholesome and unwholesome deeds, which they class by mind, speech and body, and says she will show that they do not hold even a sesame seed's worth, beginning with the three of the mind.
526.nuance: குசல அகுசலம் (line 2) are the Buddhist terms. From here to 537 she takes the ten bad deeds in order: the three of the mind (527-530), then the four of speech (531-537), the list the Manimekalai's teacher gives (Manimekalai 30, lines 64-70).

claims.claim: good and bad deeds are done by mind, speech and body

527.reading: Neelakesi argues that if all wanting is coveting, then the whole garland of verses the Buddha strung together is coveting too, and he does not see even this.
527.nuance: The target is the first mental fault, வெஃகல். Lines 2-3 (தீண்டல் அன்ன, தீண்டிய வந்தவோ) are hard to construe; the charge read here, that the teacher's own wish to teach is a wanting, rests on line 2.

claims.claim: all wanting is coveting, a fault of the mind
if every wanting is coveting, the teacher's own composing of his teaching is coveting

528.reading: Neelakesi says that since the Buddha does not declare that coveting the good is good and coveting what is not good is not, he must now state a rule under which his word 'coveting' is free of evil.
528.nuance: She asks for coveting to be judged by its object. மனமை (line 2) is probably a slip for அன்மை, which the parallel with நன்மை requires.

claims.claim: wanting what is good is not a fault; coveting must be judged by its object

529.reading: Neelakesi says deceit, pride and greed, which are of the mind, are as evil as anger, yet the Buddha, though he saw them, did not condemn them; that is his fraud, and once these are admitted others follow.
529.nuance: மாயம் மானம் உலோபம் with வெகுளி (lines 1-2) make the Jain four passions: anger, pride, deceit and greed. The charge is that the Buddhist list of mental faults (coveting, anger, wrong view) leaves three of them out.

claims.claim: anger is a fault of the mind
deceit, pride and greed are faults of the mind as evil as anger

530.reading: Neelakesi grants that right view is the excellence above all seeing, but argues that whoever wants it, judging it good, wants it from desire, and so by the Buddhist rule falls while assenting to it.
530.nuance: காட்சி is the third mental item (பொல்லாக் காட்சி, wrong view, in the Buddhist list), and also the Jain right vision. Line 4 (வழித்தனன்) is obscure, so the conclusion is read from the run of argument in 527-528.

claims.claim: right view is the highest excellence of seeing
wanting right view is itself a wanting, so the Buddhist rule on coveting condemns it

531.reading: Neelakesi recalls that the Buddhists declared lying, slander, harsh words and idle talk to be the four evil deeds of the tongue, and their opposites good.
531.nuance: The list is the Buddhist one as the Manimekalai gives it, almost word for word (பொய்யே குறளை கடுஞ்சொல் பயன் இல், Manimekalai 30, line 68). குறள்ளே and கொனைதல் (lines 1-2) are probably faulty.

claims.claim: lying, slander, harsh words and idle talk are the four evil deeds of speech

532.reading: Neelakesi lists composite things: begging bowl, water pot, mansion, monastery, house, topknot, ascetic's vessel, robe, pot, shop, food, bed, body and soul, and all other things made of parts.
532.nuance: The list runs straight into 533, and mixes the monk's own goods (மண்டை, குண்டிகை, கூறை) with the body and soul, so that his daily speech is caught by the argument.

533.reading: Neelakesi argues that if all these are only names for collections with no single thing there, yet the Buddhist names them again and again, he cannot establish true speech, and his own rule against lying condemns him.
533.nuance: This is where the two halves of the sarukkam meet: the doctrine that composites are only names (532) is set against the rule that lying is a bad deed of speech (531). The vocative விளி நாச (line 4) is obscure.

claims.claim: composite things are only names for collections, with no single thing there
one who names what he holds unreal speaks falsely every time he names it

534.reading: Neelakesi mocks the red-robed one who says earth, water, the great city, vessels, wind, fire, forest and clan are all false, saying that of all this only his own deceit is not false.
534.nuance: The list of elements and goods called பொய் is the Jain account of Buddhist teaching; the Buddhists would say such things exist by convention, not that they are lies. Line 4 (சலம் பொய் அன்று, சத்தை) is read as sarcasm, but its exact turn is uncertain.

claims.claim: earth, water, fire, wind and all made things are unreal

535.reading: Neelakesi says that besides slander, which the Buddhists call a fault, there are many other unworthy kinds of speech, such as talking alone with a woman and teaching the arts of pleasure, and harsh words must be guarded against as well.
535.nuance: The objection is that the four-item list is too short; her examples come from a renouncer's code of speech rather than from the Buddhist list.

claims.claim: the faults of speech are many more than four, including private talk with a woman and teaching pleasures

536.reading: Neelakesi argues that if speaking gently is a good deed, then those who softly lay plans to wound and kill, and the whispered counsels that urge such deeds, would be upright.
536.nuance: She refutes the rule that soft speech is good by the gentle-voiced plotter: the goodness of speech lies in what it brings about, not its tone. மந்திரம் (line 3) is counsel, not a sacred formula. Line 2 is compressed.

claims.claim: gentle speech is a good deed
soft words that plot harm are not good, so speech is not good by its gentleness

537.reading: Neelakesi asks who would condemn as harsh the stern words that restrain, and whether saying 'give' is not wholesome, and calls the Buddhist teaching a wicked lesson that brings its holder down.
537.nuance: Lines 1-2 are obscure (கடுக்கத் தாமடிகள், ஒடுக்கச் சாம்பிவை); the reading that a harsh word may restrain, as 'give' is good whatever its tone, is tentative.

claims.claim: urging another to give is a wholesome deed of speech

links.note: In 203 Neelakesi told Kundalakesi that a power carried from moment to moment would be a sixth thing beyond the aggregates; in 513 she says the Buddha's store of consciousness is the soul under another name.
links.teaches: Across two opponents the Jain argument has one shape: any carrier the Buddhist adds to explain memory and continuity is called a soul, so the store-consciousness is met with the charge first made against Kundalakesi.

links.note: 201 argues that if nothing of the first moment remains in the next, knowing is impossible; 518 tests this on hearing a word letter by letter.
links.teaches: The general continuity objection becomes a concrete test the opponent cannot dodge: no one could even understand the word 'Buddha' if each letter's knower perished before the next.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives the joined name as a valid mode of speech: many letters coming together appear as a word; 518 says a momentary mind could never put the letters together.
links.teaches: The two epics take the same example, a word made of letters, to opposite ends: the Buddhist treats it as a correct conventional name, the Jain as proof that something must last to join the letters.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher counts the collective name (the body, water, a country) as a true mode of speech; 533 says naming collections one holds unreal makes every such word a lie.
links.teaches: The Jain charge of lying presupposes that a name must match one real thing, which is the very premise the Buddhist account of conventional naming in the Manimekalai rejects.

links.note: The Manimekalai names the mind's three bad deeds as coveting, anger and wrong view; 529 says pride, deceit and greed are as evil as anger and the Buddhists leave them uncondemned.
links.teaches: Set against the Buddhist epic's actual list, Neelakesi's charge turns out to be a clash of classifications: she measures a list of ten deeds against the Jain four passions, anger, pride, deceit and greed.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives exactly four bad deeds of speech in a closed list of ten; 535 says there are many more, such as talking alone with a woman.
links.teaches: Neelakesi quotes the Buddhist list faithfully and attacks its closure, not its content: her additions come from a renouncer's code of conduct, which a list of ten deeds for all people does not try to cover.

links.note: Kural 35 sets aside envy, craving, anger and harsh words as the four that virtue avoids; 529 names anger, pride, deceit and greed as the faults of the mind.
links.teaches: Both make anger and greed central, but each completes the list from its own school: the Kural adds envy and a fault of speech, the Jain debater pride and deceit, so the shared pair is common ground and the rest is sectarian.

gains.a: the Jain list of passions is shown to share its core with a widely accepted ethical rule, which strengthens her charge that the Buddhists left faults out
gains.b: the couplet's list is shown not to be the only fourfold reckoning; a Jain debater would count pride and deceit where it counts envy and harsh speech

links.note: 533 holds that naming a thing one thinks unreal is a lie; Kural 292 holds that even a falsehood stands as truth if it yields faultless good.
links.teaches: Neelakesi's charge only works on a test of truth by match with things; on the Kural's test by effect, the Buddhist's conventional names, harming no one, would not be lies at all.

gains.a: the verse's assumption about what truth is becomes visible as an assumption, one a widely read ethics book does not share
gains.b: the couplet's measure of truth by its fruit is shown to settle a philosophical dispute about speech that it never names

links.note: Kural 91 defines sweet words as moist with love and free of deceit; 536 argues against a rule that gentle speech is good by citing the soft-spoken plotter.
links.teaches: The Kural's definition already builds in the guard Neelakesi says the Buddhist rule lacks: speech counts as sweet only when it is without deceit, so her gentle conspirator would not qualify under it.

gains.a: the objection gets a ready answer in an older definition, which shows the rule can be repaired rather than discarded
gains.b: the couplet's clause படிறிலவாம் is shown to do real work, excluding exactly the soft-spoken plotter a debater raised

links.note: 534 mocks the teacher who calls earth, water, fire and city false; Pambatti Siddhar bids the reader be clear that the world is false and dance.
links.teaches: The Jain realist's retort, that one who calls all things false leaves no ground for his own truth, falls on the Siddhar's world-is-false as much as on the Buddhist's, though the Siddhar makes it a release-giving insight, not a doctrine to defend.

gains.a: the verse's attack is shown to reach beyond Buddhism to a Tamil Saiva-Vedantic saying that also calls the world false
gains.b: the Siddhar's flat statement meets the objection it never answers: how one who calls the world false still claims his own words are true

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: label from earlier chapters (194, 200); these verses use the aggregates' words (கந்தங்கள் 519, குறி 521-525)

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: புத்தன் (519); also வாமன் (517)

new_concepts.gloss: a sense faculty; in Jain teaching beings are graded by how many of the five senses they have
formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id differs from vaadham, which the list already uses for alchemy

source_issues: 515 line 3: யாலாக்கிய and ஒருவாப் பாக்கியம் are hard to construe.
517 lines 3-4: முற்றறிவின் றீத்தனை does not yield a clear comparison.
518 line 1: பிரிவின்கணாறாம் பெயர் நுனது is obscure.
521 line 4: கேள ends without its final vowel sign (for கேளாய் or கேண்மோ), probably a slip.
522 line 2: காடின் gives no sense, probably corrupt.
527-530: the e-text's '•' was repaired to ஃ (வெஃகுதல், இஃது, அஃது).
528 line 2: மனமை is probably a slip for அன்மை.
531 lines 1-2: குறள்ளே (for குறளை) and கொனைதல் are probably faulty.
537 lines 1-2: கடுக்கத் தாமடி கள்ளெனக் காய்ஞர்யா ரொடுக்கச் சாம்பிவை is obscure.
